questions.question: Take ----- time.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
Take time. ___
The verb “Take” is reflexive in this context, meaning you are doing the action for yourself.
The correct reflexive pronoun is “yourself.”
So the correct sentence is:
Take time yourself.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. you → Does not reflect the action back to the subject → grammatically incorrect.
B. your → Possessive adjective → cannot stand alone → incorrect.
C. you're → Contraction of “you are” → does not fit → incorrect.

questions.question: I really like the way that car looks, but ----- price is more than I can afford.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
I really like the way that car looks, but ___ price is more than I can afford.
We need a pronoun to refer back to “that car”.
The correct possessive pronoun is “its” (not listed in the options correctly, but assuming A. it was intended to be “its”).
So the correct sentence should read:
I really like the way that car looks, but its price is more than I can afford.
❌ Why others are wrong:
B. it's → Contraction of “it is” → grammatically incorrect here.
C. it has → Verb phrase → incorrect.
D. it → Same as A; but context requires possessive → should be “its.”

questions.question: Youth, I do adore thee'. What is the meaning of the word 'thee' in this line ?[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The line is:
"Youth, I do adore thee."
“Thee” is an archaic English pronoun used in older English poetry and literature.
It is the objective case of “thou”, meaning “you”” when the person is the object of the verb.
So the sentence means:
Youth, I do adore you.
❌ Why others are wrong:
B. them → Refers to multiple people → incorrect, “thee” is singular.
C. your → Possessive → incorrect.
D. yours → Possessive pronoun → incorrect.

questions.question: My father never approved of ----- a foreigner.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
My father never approved of ___ a foreigner.
After “approve of”, we use a gerund (verb + ing) when expressing an action.
“Her marrying” is a gerund phrase acting as the object of “approved of.”
So the correct sentence is:
My father never approved of her marrying a foreigner.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. her to marry → After “approve of,” we don’t use the infinitive → incorrect.
C. she marrying → Subject pronoun “she” is incorrect here; we need object + gerund → “her marrying.”
D. she not marry → Wrong structure → not a gerund phrase → incorrect

questions.question: If you insist ----- you must pay my money.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
If you insist, you must pay ___ my money.
The expression “insist on” is followed by a noun or gerund (verb + ing).
“My coming” is a gerund phrase acting as the object of “insist on.”
So the correct sentence is:
If you insist, you must pay on my coming my money.
(More naturally in standard English: “If you insist, you must pay me when I come.”)
❌ Why others are wrong:
B. me to come → “Insist me to come” is grammatically incorrect; “insist on” is needed.
C. on me to come → Incorrect form; after “insist on,” we use gerund, not infinitive.
D. so that I come → Changes the meaning; not the correct grammatical structure.

questions.question: We insist on ----- leaving the room.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
We insist on ___ leaving the room.
The verb phrase “insist on” is followed by a gerund (leaving).
The object of the gerund is the person performing the action, so we use “to you” to indicate who should leave.
So the correct sentence is:
We insist on your leaving the room. ✅

questions.question: When friends insist on ----- expensive gifts, it makes most people uncomfortable.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
When friends insist on expensive gifts, it makes most people uncomfortable.
We are focusing on the phrase:
it makes most people uncomfortable ___
After “makes someone uncomfortable,” we use a gerund phrase to indicate the action causing discomfort.
To show possession (the action belongs to “them”), we use the possessive pronoun + gerund → “their accepting.”
So the correct sentence is:
When friends insist on expensive gifts, it makes most people uncomfortable their accepting. ✅

questions.question: My dog is smarter than -----.[]
questions.explanation:
A. their ❌ → “their” is a possessive adjective. It must be followed by a noun (their dog).
B. theirs ✅ → Correct possessive pronoun (stands alone).
C. your ❌ → Possessive adjective; needs a noun.
D. her ❌ → Object pronoun; does not show possession.
Rule:
Possessive adjective → my, your, his, her, their (needs a noun)
Possessive pronoun → mine, yours, his, hers, theirs (no noun needed)

questions.question: Is that my key, or is it -----.[]
questions.explanation:
A. the yours? ❌ → Incorrect structure
B. they your's? ❌ → Wrong grammar and spelling (your's is incorrect)
C. your? ❌ → “your” is a possessive adjective and must be followed by a noun
Rule:
your → possessive adjective (needs a noun)
yours → possessive pronoun (stands alone)
Example:
This book is mine.
That house is theirs.
Is this pen yours?

questions.question: Our laboratory is much more spacious than -----.[]
questions.explanation:
10A. you ❌ → Subject pronoun; not possessive
B. him ❌ → Object pronoun; not possessive
C. their ❌ → Possessive adjective; must be followed by a noun (their laboratory)
D. hers ✅ → Possessive pronoun; correct
Rule:
When a noun is omitted after comparison, use a possessive pronoun:
mine
yours
his
hers

questions.question: You should not say nasty things about Jessica. She is a friend of -----.[]
questions.explanation:
11A. her ❌ → Object pronoun; incorrect in this structure
B. you ❌ → Subject pronoun; not possessive
C. ours ✅ → Correct possessive pronoun
D. me ❌ → Object pronoun; incorrect
Rule:
After “a friend of”, use a possessive pronoun:
a friend of mine
a cousin of hers

questions.question: ------ among you would like to go first ?[]
questions.explanation:
12Who → subject of the verb “would like” ✅
Whom → object of a verb or preposition ❌
Which → used to select from a specific set, but less natural here ❌
Whose → shows possession ❌
Rule:
Use who when referring to the subject of a sentence.
Use whom when referring to the object of a verb or preposition.
Example:
Who is coming to the party? (subject)
Whom did you invite? (object)

questions.question: The first hall of the game belonged to us, the second half to -----.[]
questions.explanation:
13The phrase “belonged to ___” requires an object pronoun because the pronoun is the object of the preposition “to.”
Object pronouns are: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
“They” is a subject pronoun, so it’s wrong.
“Their” is a possessive adjective, which doesn’t fit here.
“Those” is a demonstrative pronoun, which also doesn’t make sense in this context.
So the sentence correctly reads:
"The first half of the game belonged to us, the second half to them." ✅

questions.question: He is a liar.Do you trust ----- ?[]
questions.explanation:
14
The verb trust requires an object (someone whom the trust is directed toward) .
In English, him is the objective case of "he," used as the object of a verb.
So the sentence correctly becomes:
"He is a liar. Do you trust him?" ✅
Other options explained:
his → possessive adjective, not used as an object.
her → refers to a female, but "he" is male.
he → nominative case, used as the subject, not the object

questions.question: Didn't you know that it ----- who played the joke ?[]
questions.explanation:
15"Didn't you know that it was we who played the joke?" ✅
Why the others are wrong:
was us → "us" is objective; after linking verbs, we use nominative, not objective.
were us / were we → "were" does not agree with singular it; the verb must be was.

questions.question: The captain, ----- had a score of 30.[]
questions.explanation:
16"The captain, Joy and I, had a score of 30." ✅
Why the other options are wrong:
Joy and me → “me” is objective; not used as the subject.
Joy and us → “us” is objective; incorrect here.
Joy and myself → “myself” is reflexive; only used when referring back to the subject (“I hurt myself”), not as a simple subject.

questions.question: Let ----- introduce ----- to -----.[]
questions.explanation:
“Let me introduce to you, him…” ✅
Why the other options are wrong:
A. my, your, his → these are possessive adjectives, not objects.
C. mine, yours, he → “mine” and “yours” are possessive pronouns; “he” is nominative (subject), not object.
D. him, she, their → “she” is nominative; “their” is possessive adjective; not correct for objects.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.[]
options: The presents are for you and me
The presents are for you and I
The presents are for me and you
The presents are for I and we
questions.explanation:
"The presents are for ___."
The preposition for requires an object pronoun, not a subject pronoun.
Objective pronouns are: me, you, him, her, us, them.
So the sentence becomes:
"The presents are for you and me." ✅
Why the others are wrong:
B. you and I → “I” is nominative (subject), but after for, we need the object me.
C. me and you → grammatically correct, but stylistically it’s polite to put the other person first: “you and me”.
D. I and we → both are subject pronouns; incorrect after “for.”

questions.question: Find out the correct sentence.[]
options: I insist you to go there
I insist on your going there
I insist upon you to go there
I insist yourself to go there
questions.explanation:
“Insist” is followed by:
on + noun/gerund → correct form
Example: I insist on your coming early. ✅
The other options are grammatically wrong:
A. I insist you to go there → “insist” does not take “you to [verb]”; that’s incorrect.
C. I insist upon you to go there → same mistake; “upon” is fine, but “you to go” is wrong.
D. I insist yourself to go there → “yourself” is reflexive and cannot be used here.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
questions.explanation:
"___ are present."
The subject of the sentence is “He and I”.
For subjects, we must use nominative case pronouns: I, he, she, we, they.
The verb must agree with a plural subject, so we use are.
✅ Correct sentence: "He and I are present."

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.[]
options: I, you and he are to blame
I, you and he should obey our teacher
He, you and I are to blame
questions.explanation:
✅ Correct sentence: “I, you and he are to blame.”
Why the other options are less suitable:
B. I, you and he should obey our teacher → grammatically correct, but it’s a different meaning; the question asks specifically about blame.
C. He, you and I are to blame → also correct grammatically; sometimes ordering subjects is about politeness: “I” often comes last, so this could also be acceptable.
D. You and I are guilty → incomplete; it leaves out “he.”

questions.question: It was ----- came running into the classroom.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: "It was he who came running into the classroom."
Here’s why:
After “It is/was”, the pronoun should be in the subjective case (he, she, I, we) because it is technically the subject of the verb in the relative clause “who came running…”.
So even though “him” feels natural in speech, grammatically “he” is correct.
A quick tip: If you expand the sentence to “He came running into the classroom”, you can see why he is the right choice.

questions.question: All of us Abir, Wafi, Nibir, Aritro and ----- were present.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: "All of us — Abir, Wafi, Nibir, Aritro, and I — were present."
Here’s why:
After “and” in a list that includes yourself as part of the subject of the verb “were present”, you must use the subjective case, which is “I”.
Using “me” or “mine” would be incorrect because they are objective and possessive forms, not subjects.
A simple trick: remove the other names:
“I was present” ✅
“Me was present” ❌

questions.question: Shamim and ----- are going to the cinema.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: "Shamim and I are going to the cinema."
Here’s why:
The pronoun is part of the subject of the verb “are going”, so you need the subjective case, which is “I”.
“Me” would be wrong because it’s an object, not a subject.
“My” is possessive, and “myself” is reflexive, both of which don’t fit here.
Quick tip: Remove the other person to check:
“I am going to the cinema” ✅
“Me am going to the cinema” ❌

questions.question: The woman asked me where the hotel was so I told ----- how to get there.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence is: "The woman asked me where the hotel was, so I told her how to get there."
Here’s why:
After “told”, the pronoun should be in the objective case because it’s the indirect object of the verb.
“Her” is the correct objective case form for “she”.
The other options don’t fit:
“She” → subjective (wrong here)
“Them” → plural (wrong)
“It” → refers to things, not a person

questions.question: কোনটি reflexive pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
The answer is: “Myself”.
Here’s why:
Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and the object of a sentence are the same. Examples: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
Each → indefinite pronoun
Who → interrogative or relative pronoun
He → personal pronoun
Example:
“I hurt myself while cooking.” ✅
The action comes back to the subject, so myself is reflexive.

questions.question: Which one is a reflexive pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject of the sentence. Examples: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
Me → personal/objective pronoun
They → personal/subject pronoun
Self → just the noun “self,” not a complete reflexive pronoun
Example:
“He looked at himself in the mirror.” ✅
The action reflects back on the subject he, so we use himself.

questions.question: Which one is a reflexive pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and object are the same. Examples: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
That → demonstrative pronoun
You → personal pronoun
Both is tricky, but in this context, only “yourself” is reflexive.
Example:
“You should take care of yourself.” ✅

questions.question: Myself' is a/an ---[]
questions.explanation:
“Myself” is a reflexive pronoun because it refers back to the subject of the sentence.
Examples of reflexive pronouns: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
It is not just a pronoun, because it specifically reflects the action back to the subject.
Example:
“I taught myself to play the piano.” ✅

questions.question: Do it yourself. What kind of pronoun 'yourself' is ---[]
questions.explanation:
In the sentence “Do it yourself”, the word “yourself” refers back to the subject “you”, emphasizing that you are the one doing the action.
A reflexive pronoun is used when the subject and the object of a verb are the same person or thing.
Common reflexive pronouns: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves.

questions.question: What kind of pronoun 'himself' is ---[]
questions.explanation:
The pronoun “himself” is a reflexive pronoun because it refers back to the subject of the sentence.
Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and the object of the verb are the same.
Example: He taught himself to play the piano.
Here, “himself” refers back to “He”, showing that he did the action on himself.

questions.question: He killed himself'. Here 'himself' is ---[]
questions.explanation:
the sentence “He killed himself”, the word “himself” is a reflexive pronoun because:
It refers back to the subject “He”.
It shows that the action of the verb affects the same person who performs it.
So the correct answer is C. Reflexive pronoun.

questions.question: Pinocchio is hungry and looks for an egg to cook ----- an omelet but to his surprise, the omelet flies out of the window.[]
questions.explanation:
the sentence, “Pinocchio is hungry and looks for an egg to cook an omelet but to his surprise, the omelet flies out of the window,” the correct pronoun to refer back to Pinocchio is “himself”.
“Himself” is a reflexive pronoun because it refers back to the subject Pinocchio.
It shows that Pinocchio is the one performing or affected by the action in relation to himself.

questions.question: Nobody likes her. She talks about ----- all the time.[]
questions.explanation:
the sentence “Nobody likes her. She talks about ---- all the time,” the correct choice is “herself.”
“Herself” is a reflexive pronoun because it refers back to the subject “She”.
Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and object of the action are the same person.

questions.question: Control -----, Sabah ! Everything is fine, so don't start crying.[]
questions.explanation:
In the sentence “Control -----, Sabah! Everything is fine, so don't start crying,” the correct pronoun is “yourself.”
“Yourself” is a reflexive pronoun because it refers back to the person being spoken to, Sabah.
Reflexive pronouns are often used in imperative sentences (commands) to emphasize that the action should be done by the person addressed.

questions.question: Control ----- Farhana ! Don't get hysterical.[]
questions.explanation:
In “Control ----- Farhana! Don’t get hysterical,” the pronoun must refer back to Farhana, the person being addressed.
“Yourself” is a reflexive pronoun, which is used when the action refers back to the subject (here, Farhana).
Using “you”, “oneself”, or “self” would be grammatically incorrect in this context.

questions.question: He wanted nobody ----- to know ----- the treasure was hidden.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence “He wanted nobody know ----- the treasure was hidden” is completed as:
“He wanted nobody know but himself where the treasure was hidden.”
“Himself” is a reflexive pronoun, referring back to the subject he.
“Where” correctly introduces the location of the treasure.

questions.question: A snake can eat and digest animals much larger than -----.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence “A snake can eat and digest animals much larger than -----” is correctly completed as:
“A snake can eat and digest animals much larger than itself.”
“Itself” is a reflexive pronoun, referring back to the subject “a snake”.
Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and the object of comparison or action are the same.

questions.question: I certainly esteem ----- as a steady, reasonable kind of person.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence “I certainly esteem steady, reasonable kind of ----- as a person” is correctly completed as:
“I certainly esteem steady, reasonable kind of myself as a person.”
“Myself” is a reflexive pronoun, referring back to the subject “I”.
Reflexive pronouns are used when the subject and the object are the same person, often for emphasis.

questions.question: Masud introduced ----- to the other guests.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence “Masud introduced the other guests -----” is completed as:
“Masud introduced the other guests to himself.”
“Himself” is a reflexive pronoun, referring back to the subject Masud.
Reflexive pronouns are used when the action relates back to the subject, even in contexts like introducing others in relation to oneself.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: I shall avail myself of this opportunity
questions.explanation:
The correct sentence is: “I shall avail myself of this opportunity.”
The verb “avail” is always used reflexively in English. You cannot say “I shall avail this opportunity” directly.
The structure is: “subject + avail + oneself of + opportunity/benefit”.
Example: She availed herself of the library resources.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: He absented himself from the meeting
He was absented from the meeting
He had absented from the meeting
questions.explanation:
The correct sentence is: “He absented himself from the meeting.”
The verb “absent” is used reflexively in English.
You cannot simply say “He absented from the meeting”; it must be “absent himself from…”
Structure: subject + absent + oneself + from + place/event.
Example: She absented herself from school yesterday.

questions.question: This is my pen. That is yours. Here 'This' and 'That' are ---[]
questions.explanation:
In the sentence “This is my pen. That is yours,” the words “This” and “That” are demonstrative pronouns.
Demonstrative pronouns are used to point out specific things.
Examples: this, that, these, those.
Here:
“This” refers to the pen near the speaker.
“That” refers to the pen farther away or being pointed at.

questions.question: Which of the following is demonstrative pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
The demonstrative pronoun among the options is “Those.”
Demonstrative pronouns are used to point out specific things or people.
Examples: this, that, these, those.
Here, “Those” refers to specific items or people that are farther away or plural.

questions.question: Modern farms are much larger than ----- of former times.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence “Modern farms are much larger than ----- of former times” is correctly completed as:
“Modern farms are much larger than those of former times.”
“Those” is a demonstrative pronoun used to refer to plural nouns mentioned or implied earlier (here, the farms of former times).
You cannot use “that” (singular) or “this/these” (wrong context) in this sentence.

questions.question: The students of Bangladesh are more meritorious than ----- of the USA.[]
questions.explanation:
The sentence “The students of Bangladesh are more meritorious than ----- of the USA” is correctly completed as:
“The students of Bangladesh are more meritorious than those of the USA.”
“Those” is a demonstrative pronoun used to refer to plural nouns mentioned or implied earlier (here, the students of the USA).
“That” would be singular, and “all” or “another” do not fit the comparison context.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: The sceneries of Chittagong are better than Dhaka
The sceneries of Chittagong are better than that of Dhaka
The scenery of Chittagong are better than that of Dhaka
The scenery of Chittagong are better than Dhaka
questions.explanation:
“The scenery of Chittagong is better than that of Dhaka.”
Here’s why:
“Scenery” is an uncountable noun, so we use the singular form: “the scenery of Chittagong”.
Comparison requires the singular “that” to refer back to the uncountable noun from Dhaka: “than that of Dhaka.”
The verb should be “is” (not “are”) because the subject “scenery” is singular.

questions.question: The climate of Dinajpur is like ----- of Rangpur. []
questions.explanation:
The sentence “The climate of Dinajpur is like ----- of Rangpur” is correctly completed as:
“The climate of Dinajpur is like that of Rangpur.”
“That” is a demonstrative pronoun used here to refer back to “climate” (a singular noun) of Rangpur.
Using “the” or “as” directly would be grammatically incorrect in this context.

questions.question: Your advice is 'no different from' the other friends.[]
options: not different from that of the
questions.explanation:
The sentence “Your advice is 'no different from' the other friends” is correctly written as:
“Your advice is not different from that of the other friends.”
“That” is a demonstrative pronoun referring back to “advice”.
Since “advice” is singular and uncountable, we cannot just say “the other friends”; we must use “that of the other friends” to compare the advice itself.

questions.question: Your courage is 'as great as any other person' in defending your country.[]
options: as great as any other person
as great as any other persons
as great as that of any other person
questions.explanation:
The sentence “Your courage is 'as great as any other person' in defending your country” is correctly written as:
“Your courage is as great as that of any other person in defending your country.”
“That” is a demonstrative pronoun referring to “courage”, not the person.
Using “any other person” directly would incorrectly compare a person to a quality.
Correct comparison: courage (your quality) → that (of other persons’ courage).
